Dear Members,
On behalf of the Board of Directors, it is our privilege to present 
the 50th Annual Report and 7th Integrated Annual Report of NTPC 
Limited (‘NTPC’ or Company) for the Financial Year ended 31st 
March 2026 along with the Audited Standalone and Consolidated Financial Statements for the Financial Year ended 31
st March 2026, 
the Auditors’ report, and comments of the Comptroller and Auditor 
General (C&AG) of India on the financial statements thereon. 
The Company continued to align its growth strategy with the nation’s 
long-term development aspirations by delivering reliable, sustainable and future-ready energy solutions during FY 2025-26.
India’s aspiration of becoming a developed nation under the vision 
of Viksit Bharat 2047  places the power sector at the centre of 
economic growth, industrial competitiveness and energy transition. Reflecting the sector’s strategic importance, NITI Aayog’s recent 
Viksit Bharat and Net Zero report also reaffirms that 
“India’s power 
sector is central to the nation’s economic growth and development.”  
As India’s largest integrated power utility, your Company remains committed to supporting this national vision by ensuring reliable, 
affordable and sustainable electricity while strengthening the 
country’s energy security. Building on its leadership in baseload generation, NTPC is transforming into a future-ready energy major through investments 
in renewable energy, nuclear power, energy storage and digital technologies. In line with its long-term growth strategy, the Company 
aims to achieve 149 GW of installed capacity at the group level by 
2032. This includes increasing renewable energy (RE) capacity to 60 GW and its share in installed capacity to 44% from 13% as on 
31
st March 2026. With nuclear power expected to support India’s 
transition to a low-carbon energy future, your Company is targeting 0.7 GW of nuclear capacity by 2032.
By 2037, your Company plans to lead India’s energy transition by 
reaching 244 GW of installed capacity at the group level, including 136 GW of RE capacity representing 56% of total installed capacity, 
and 6.3 GW of nuclear capacity.
To support grid-level storage requirements from higher RE 
integration, your Company plans to develop BESS capacity of 22 
GWh by 2032 and 52 GWh by 2037, along with PSP capacity of 1 
GW by 2032 and 6.2 GW by 2037.

9. Pr oject Managem ent
Your Company follows a robust Integrated Project Management 
and Control System (IPMCS) for planning, execution, monitoring and control of its projects. The framework integrates the efforts of various stakeholders, including Government agencies, financing institutions, contractors, 
vendors and internal functional groups, with the objective of 
ensuring timely commissioning of projects within the approved cost parameters while maintaining the highest standards of 
safety and quality.
The IPMCS is supported by a structured governance framework 
comprising Engineering Management, Quality Assurance & 
Inspection, Contract Management and Site Management Control Centres, which work in close coordination with support 
functions such as Finance, Human Resources, Operations 
Services, Corporate Planning and Information Technology. Leveraging technology-enabled planning and monitoring 
tools, the framework facilitates dynamic scheduling, effective 
interface management and continuous review of project milestones, thereby enabling integrated project implementation 
and control under the overall guidance of Director (Projects).
Further details on the Company’s project management and 
execution framework are provided in the ‘Manufactured Capital’ 
section of the Integrated Annual Report. 
(Refer page no. 58)

12.1  Str ategic Diversification – Increasing Self-Reliance
 In its endea vor to strengthen long-term competitiveness and 
create sustainable value, your Company has progressively 
diversified its business portfolio to emerge as an integrated 
energy major with a presence across the entire power value chain. Through strategic backward and forward integration into 
areas such as coal mining, power equipment manufacturing, power trading and distribution, the Company continues to 
enhance its operational resilience and self-reliance while 
actively evaluating emerging business opportunities aligned with its long-term growth strategy. Y our Company is also pursuing opportunities to strengthen 
and diversify its generation portfolio and unlock value through strategic investments and acquisitions. In line with this 
approach, NTPC in consortium with Maharashtra State Power

on 24
th February 2026 through the resolution process under 
the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016, as approved by the 
National Company Law Tribunal (NCL T).
 In addition to expanding its presence within the conventional 
power segment through strategic acquisitions, your Company 
also made significant progress in emerging energy technologies 
during FY 2025-26 as part of its strategy to support India’s energy 
transition and build a future-ready energy portfolio. During the year, key milestones were achieved in nuclear energy, pumped 
storage and BESS, including the laying of the foundation stone

16. Financing  of New Projects / Capital Expenditure
During FY 2025-26, the Group capital expenditure (CAPEX), 
including Joint Ventures and Subsidiaries, rose to ₹55,985.82 
crore, making a notable increase from ₹48,594.59 crore in FY 2024-25. On a standalone basis, CAPEX recorded strong growth reaching ₹26,082.85 crore from ₹23,664.59 crore in the 
previous year, on accrual basis.Your Company continues to adopt a prudent and well-defined 
financing strategy to support its capacity expansion and long-term growth plans. The funding structure for various projects is 
aligned with their underlying business characteristics, generally 
following a debt-equity ratio of 70:30 for thermal, hydro and coal mining projects and 80:20 for renewable energy projects. 
The Board is confident that the Company’s strong internal 
accruals will adequately support the equity requirements for upcoming projects.
With a low-geared capital structure and robust credit ratings, 
your Company is well-positioned to secure the necessary borrowings. It continues to explore both domestic and 
international funding avenues, including overseas development 
assistance from bilateral agencies, to mobilize debt for its planned capacity expansion.
Additionally, your Company actively undertakes debt swapping 
for domestic loans, strategically replacing high-interest loans 
with lower-cost borrowings to optimize the overall cost of 
debt. Continuous engagement and negotiation with banks to further reduce interest rates remain a key focus, enabling 
your Company to keep borrowing costs competitive and 
strengthening financial efficiency.

The Company continues to pursue R&M of its ageing 
generating thermal power units as a key strategic initiative to 
enhance asset longevity, operational reliability, and sustainable 
performance. R&M interventions are undertaken for units that have completed or are nearing 25 years of commercial 
operation, with the objective of extending their useful life 
and ensuring continued safe, efficient, and environmentally 
compliant operation.
The program focuses on replacement of obsolete equipment, 
refurbishment of critical systems, and deployment of modern technologies to improve plant reliability, availability, efficiency, and maintainability. It also supports compliance with evolving 
statutory, environmental, and grid management requirements.
Through a structured and phased approach to modernization, 
the Company aims to mitigate the impact of asset ageing and technological obsolescence, optimize the life-cycle performance of its generating assets, and ensure their reliable contribution to the nation’s energy security.

Sustainable development remains an integral part of your Company’s long-term business strategy and value creation framework. Guided by its commitment to responsible and sustainable growth, the Company continues to integrate Environmental, Social and Governance (ESG) principles across its operations and business processes through a structured ESG Management System (ESG-MS), supported by strategic oversight of the Board-level ESG and Climate Change Committee.

20. Fly As h Utilization
Ash generated from coal-based thermal power plants is 
a valuable resource for the cement industry, construction sector, and manufacturers of building materials. It is widely 
utilized in cement manufacturing, road construction, 
flyover embankments, mine filling, and other infrastructure development activities, thereby contributing to conservation 
of natural resources and reducing degradation of fertile 
agricultural land. Various innovative initiatives and sustainable practices are also being undertaken to enhance overall ash 
utilization across NTPC stations.
Sust ainable ash utilization continues to remain a key focus 
area for all NTPC coal-based power stations. To strengthen and 
streamline these efforts, NTPC has established a dedicated Ash 
Utilization Group at Corporate Centre, supported by station-
level teams responsible for effective planning, monitoring, and 
implementation of ash utilization activities. NTPC remains 
committed towards sustaining 100% ash utilization in line with 
statutory guidelines and environmental stewardship objectives. 
Project-wise details of ash generation and utilization are 
provided at Annexure-IX of this Report.

24. Risk Management
Your Company has established a robust Enterprise Risk Management (ERM) framework to identify, assess, monitor 
and mitigate risks across its business operations in a 
structured and proactive manner. The framework is aligned with the requirements of the Companies Act, 2013 and SEBI 
(LODR) Regulations, 2015 and was further strengthened 
during FY 2025-26 through its revision in July 2025 to enhance alignment with the principles of ISO 31000:2018. The Board-
level Risk Management Committee (RMC) provides strategic 
oversight and periodically reviews key enterprise risks and the effectiveness of mitigation measures.
The revised ERM framework facilitates systematic 
identification and management of strategic, operational, 
financial, legal & compliance, technological and environmental 
& social risks, enabling the Company to effectively respond to the evolving business landscape. Your Company is also the 
first CPSE in the power sector to implement a comprehensive 
Business Continuity Plan (BCP) aligned with ISO 22301:2019, reinforcing its commitment towards organisational resilience 
and business continuity.
Your Company also manages its foreign exchange exposures 
through a well-defined Exchange Risk Management Policy, 
including the use of appropriate hedging instruments, to mitigate risks arising from foreign currency denominated 
borrowings and procurement contracts. During FY 2025-26, the 
Company entered into derivative contracts aggregating to JPY 15,989.65 million, USD 487.66 million and EUR 12.89 million 
towards management of foreign currency loan exposures. 
Further details on the Company’s risk management framework 
and key risk areas are provided in the ‘Risk Management’ 
section of the Integrated Annual Report.

31. W eb -based Contractors’ Labour Information and 
Management System (CLIMS) 
Your Company has successfully implemented an in-house, web-
based solution - Contractors’ Labour Information Management 
System (CLIMS) hosted on a captive private cloud. CLIMS 
streamlines key labour management processes, ensuring mandatory pre-deployment health checkups, safety training 
and compliance with statutory social security and welfare 
legislations for contract workers. The system is equipped with a fully biometric access control mechanism, enabling real-
time information on the availability of workers in various jobs 
and at the same time, augmenting the security of the power plant. Additionally, CLIMS provides contracting agencies with 
a digitised database of their workforce, facilitating efficient 
administration of wage and other statutory entitlements.
CLIMS incorporates a range of features to enhance workforce 
management. This comprehensive system enables effective 
monitoring of the digitised database of the workers engaged 
by contracting agencies and ensure coverage of the workers for statutory social security measures. By adopting CLIMS, 
your Company has improved the overall labour management 
process, facilitating overall well-being and safety of the contractors’ worker.

32.26 Performance Evaluation of the Board, Board Level 
Committees and Directors
 Ministr y of Corporate Affairs vide its notification dated 
5th June 2015 has exempted Government Companies 
from provisions of the Companies Act, 2013 relating to 
performance evaluation of the Board and its disclosure 
in the Directors’ Report. However, as a reflection of its commitment to high standards of corporate governance 
and in compliance with the applicable provisions of the 
SEBI (LODR) Regulations, 2015, during FY 2025-26, your Company has adopted a Policy on Performance Evaluation 
of the Board, Board-level Committees and Directors. 
 The e valuation framework adopted by the Company inter 
alia provide s for:• E valuation of the performance and effectiveness of 
the Board and Board-level Statutory Committees by 
all Directors individually on pre-determined criteria.
• E valuation of performance of Individual Directors, 
including Independent Directors, by the other members of the Board (excluding the Director being 
evaluated) on the basis of Strategic Leadership, 
Governance & Integrity, and Board Effectiveness etc.; and
• E valuation by the Independent Directors, at their 
separate meeting, of the performance of the Board, the Chairperson, Non-Independent Directors and the 
adequacy of the flow of information to the Board.
 Pursuant  to the said Policy, the annual performance 
evaluation of the Board, its Committees and Individual 
Directors was undertaken for FY 2025-26 at the beginning 
of FY 2026-27, and the outcome thereof was noted by the 
Board.

A Brief Profile and Performance Overview of Subsidiaries and Joint Ventures
The following provides a brief profile and performance overview of the Company’s major Joint Ventures and Subsidiaries as at  
31st March 2026.
a) Joint V enture and Subsidiary Companies in the Power Generation:
Name & Category of the Company Brief Particulars
NGEL 
(NTPC Green Energy Limited)
Material Listed SubsidiaryNGEL incorporated in April 2022, is a subsidiary of your Company and serves as its flagship 
green energy platform, spearheading the Company’s energy transition initiatives. 
The Company is engaged in the development and implementation of utility-scale solar, wind 
and hybrid power projects, including Ultra Mega Renewable Energy Power Parks (UMREPPs), across the country and is also pursuing opportunities in green hydrogen and allied emerging businesses.
Subsequent to the disinvestment of 10.99% equity stake through an Initial Public Offering (IPO) 
during FY 2024-25, your Company’s shareholding in NGEL stands at 89.01%. The balance share holding is held by public.
As on 31
st March 2026, NGEL had an aggregate operational capacity of 10,076 MW on a 
consolidated basis. During FY 2025-26, the NGEL Group (including its subsidiaries and joint 
ventures) generated 14,596 Million Units (MUs) of electricity, registering an impressive growth of 112% over the previous year, reflecting the rapid scale-up of NTPC’s renewable energy portfolio.
NEEPCO  
(North Eastern Electric Power 
Corporation Limited)
Wholly Owned SubsidiaryNEEPCO, a Mini-Ratna Category-I CPSE, became a wholly owned subsidiary of your Company 
in March 2020 upon acquisition of 100% equity stake from the Government of India. 
NEEPCO is primarily engaged in the generation and sale of electricity in the North-Eastern 
region of India and operates a diversified portfolio comprising six hydro power stations, three 
gas-based power stations and one solar power station, with an aggregate installed capacity of 2,057 MW and 1,426 MW under construction.
During FY 2025-26, NEEPCO generated 8,215.42 MUs of electricity, with hydro stations 
achieving a Plant Load Factor (PLF) of 44.53% and availability of 85.84%, while gas-based stations recorded a PLF of 48.97% and availability of 63.69%. 
NEEPCO has paid a dividend of ₹125 crore during FY 2025-26 to your Company.
THDC
(THDC India Limited)
Subsidiary with  
Government of Uttar PradeshTHDC, a Mini-Ratna Category-I CPSE, became a subsidiary of your Company in March 2020 
upon acquisition of 74.496% equity stake from the Government of India. The balance 25.504% equity stake is held by the Government of Uttar Pradesh.
THDC has a diversified portfolio comprising hydro, thermal, wind and solar power projects 
with an aggregate capacity of 5,551 MW, including 3,657 MW under operation and 1,644 MW under construction. In addition, projects aggregating approximately 10,600 MW are under various stages of feasibility studies.
During FY 2025-26, THDC recorded cumulative generation of 13,125.70 MUs.
The Tehri Hydro Power Project and Koteshwar Hydro Electric Project achieved a cumulative 
Plant Availability Factor (PAF) of 80.90%, while the Wind Power Plants and Kasargod Solar Power Project recorded Capacity Utilisation Factors (CUF) of 19.35% and 20.76%, respectively. The Dhukwan Small Hydro Electric Project achieved a PLF of 37.68%.
THDC has paid a dividend of ₹329.25 crore during FY 2025-26 to your Company.Annexure to Directors’ ReportDirectors’ Report

GLOBAL ENERGY & POWER SECTOR LANDSCAPE | FY 2025–26
The year 2025 marked a significant inflection point in the global power sector. For the first time, renewable energy accounted for 33.8% of 
total electricity generation, surpassing coal at 33.0%, signalling a structural shift in the global energy mix. Notably, clean energy sources primarily solar and wind met nearly the entire incremental electricity demand, even as the coal-based generation fell (-0.6%) for the first time 
since 2020.
This development underscores a transition that is increasingly driven by economic competitiveness and technological advancement, in 
addition to policy support, indicating that the global energy transition is entering a more self-sustaining phase.

Acceleration of Solar and Renewable Capacity Emergence of Storage as a System Enabler
Solar energy continues to be the fastest-growing source of electricity 
globally, with generation increasing by 30% year-on-year (+636 BU) in 2025. Notably, solar alone contributed approximately 75% of the 
global increase in electricity demand, supported by record capacity 
additions of ~600 GW.The rapid decline in battery pack costs globally, dropping 45% Y-o-Y to nearly $70/kWh in 2025
b, is leading to significant reduction in 
levelized cost of storage and hence driving capacity additions, and 
transforming power system dynamics. Storage technologies are 
increasingly enabling the integration of renewable energy into the grid by addressing intermittency and facilitating round-the-clock 
supply.

ECONOMIC AND SECTORAL OVERVIEW
Macroeconomic ContextIndia remained among the world’s fastest-growing major economies in FY 2025–26, with real GDP growth estimated at 7.4%, compared 
with 6.5% in FY 2024–25
c . Growth was underpinned by resilient domestic consumption, sustained public capital expenditure, improving 
rural demand, and supportive monetary conditions. Despite heightened global trade uncertainties, including tariff-related disruptions, the IMF projected India’s growth at 6.6% under its baseline scenario, reaffirming the country’s position as the fastest-growing large economy. 
During the year, the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) revised its FY 2025–26 growth forecast upward from 6.8% to 7.3%, with Q-on-Q growth for 
three straight quarters, including real GDP growth 8.2% in Q2 FY 2025-26. This resilient growth can be attributed to multiple factors such 
as robust domestic demand, rationalisation of taxes, softer crude oil prices, front-loading of Government capital expenditure, along with 
facilitative monetary and financial conditions, supported by benign inflation

Historic Milestones in FY 2025–26
• NDC target achievement ahead of schedule: India achieved 
50% non-fossil installed capacity in June 2025, five years 
ahead of its Paris Agreement target, becoming one of the few 
major economies to achieve this milestone.
• RE generation record: On 29th July 2025, renewable sources 
met 51.5% of India’s real-time electricity demand of 203 GW, 
the highest-ever intra-day RE share.
• Global RE ranking:  India became the world’s third-largest 
country by total renewable energy installed capacity (IRENA 2025), ranking third in solar (150.2 GW), fourth in wind (54.65 
GW).
• Record Non-Fossil capacity addition: Non-Fossil capacity 
addition in 2025-26 was 55.29 GW, making it the highest 
capacity addition in a single year for nuclear, large hydro and 
RE combined.
• Manufacturing scale-up: Solar Module Manufacturing Capacity has increased from 2.3 GW in 2014 to ~172 GW, as 
on 31
st March 2026; Wind Turbine Manufacturing Capacity has 
increased from 10 GW in 2014 to ~24 GW, as on 31st March 
2026.
Fuel Mix & Generation
Total electricity generation stood at approximately 1,840 BU in 
FY 2025–26, registering a modest growth of around 1% over FY 
2024–25. Thermal generation declined by about 4%, reflecting the increasing penetration of renewable energy, which displaced coal-
based generation, particularly during solar-rich periods.
Renewable electricity generation (including hydro) recorded a 
robust growth of approximately 18%, led by solar (~20% year-on-
year) and wind (~27% year-on-year). Supported by record renewable capacity additions and a favourable monsoon that moderated 
cooling demand, coal-based generation declined by around 3.7%, 
marking one of the first notable declines in recent years. Gas-based generation also declined significantly by around 18%, while nuclear 
generation witnessed a marginal reduction of approximately 3% 
during the period.Energy Storage & Grid
Energy storage deployment continued to gain momentum. As per 
the National Generation Adequacy Plan 2026 projections by the CEA, India is expected to add ~174 GW / 888 GWh of energy storage 
capacity by 2035, reflecting the growing importance of storage, not 
only for grid balancing but also for integration of rapidly increasing variable RE capacity and meet the non-solar hours’ demand.
The national transmission network expanded to approximately 
5 lakh circuit-kilometres, with inter-regional transfer capacity 
increasing to about 120 GW, enhancing grid resilience and 
facilitating renewable integration.
The National Generation Adequacy Plan 2026 has projected India’s 
peak demand to reach ~459 GW and electricity demand to ~3365 
BU by FY 2035–36, underscoring the continued requirement for substantial capacity additions across generation and grid 
infrastructure.
Distribution
The Revamped Distribution Sector Scheme (RDSS) continued to 
deliver measurable improvements in the financial and operational 
performance of distribution utilities. The ACS-ARR gap reduced 
significantly from ₹0.78/kWh in FY 2013-14 to ₹0.06/kWh in FY 2024-25, while AT&C losses reduced from 22.62% in FY 2013-14 
to 15.04% in FY 2024-25, indicating enhanced efficiency and loss 
reduction.
Legacy dues of DISCOMs also witnessed a substantial reduction, 
declining from from ₹1,39,947 crore in 2022 to just ₹3,330 crore 
by March 2026, supported by the implementation of the amended Late Payment Surcharge (LPS) Rules.
Under RDSS, smart metering has gained strong traction, with over 
19.79 crore smart meters and 52.53 lakh distribution transformer 
(DT) meters sanctioned, aimed at improving billing efficiency, 
transparency, and demand-side management. Key Policy & Regulatory Developments in FY 2025–26
During the year, several regulatory and policy developments were 
introduced to support energy transition, enhance grid flexibility, and 
strengthen market mechanisms:
• SHANTI Act, 2025:  Landmark legislation replacing the Atomic 
Energy Act 1962 & Civil Liabilities for Nuclear Damage Act, 
2010; permits private Indian companies, foreign companies (up 
to 49% FDI) and joint ventures to build, own and operate nuclear 
plants; paves the way for India’s 100 GW nuclear target by 2047.
• Scenarios Towards Viksit Bharat and Net Zero:  Sectoral 
Insights: Power by NITI Aayog (Feb 2026):  The report 
identifies rapid electrification and large-scale clean energy 
deployment as central to achieving the twin goals of India being 
a USD 30 Trillion economy by 2047 and Net Zero economy 
by 2070; projects electricity to account for nearly 60% of the 
total energy consumption by 2070, with non-fossil sources contributing about 98% of power generation; estimates 
cumulative investment requirements of approximately USD 
14.2 trillion in the power sector through 2070 and highlights affordable, reliable and low-carbon electricity as a key enabler 
of India’s long-term economic growth and decarbonisation 
pathway.
• CERC Tariff Regulations (Second Amendment), 2026: Introduced a comprehensive framework for Energy Storage 
Systems (ESS) co-located with thermal plants and ISTS. The 
regulations enable storage for supply to beneficiaries, support ancillary services, and enhance renewable energy integration. 
Key provisions include defined norms for battery life (15 years), 
RoE (14%), availability (90%), and efficiency (≥85%). Additional provisions include monthly recovery of ash transportation 
costs, incentives for captive coal mining efficiency, and 
introduction of a Regulatory Sandbox to promote innovation. 
• Thermal Unit Shutdown Framework (CERC Order, October 2025):  Allows thermal generating units to undertake unit 
shutdown (USD) when scheduled below 50% of capacity, improving operational efficiency. Restrictions on peak vs off-peak declaration ensure grid reliability. 
• Deviation Settlement Mechanism (DSM) Amendment, 2025: Provides clarity on infirm power injection and scheduling, 
including pricing caps and operational conditions, thereby 
strengthening grid discipline. 
• Virtual Power Purchase Agreements (VPPA) Guidelines, 2025:  Establishes a framework enabling consumers to 
meet RPO/RCO obligations through RECs, while facilitating renewable procurement without physical power transfer. 
• Renewable Generation Obligation (RGO) Clarification: The 
Ministry of Power has ma de RGO compliance voluntary for 
thermal stations commissioned after April 2025, providing 
greater flexibility in renewable capacity planning. • Renewable Consumption Obligation (RCO): Mandates 
increasing renewable consumption targets from ~30% in FY 
2024–25 to ~43% by FY 2029–30 for DISCOMs, open access 
consumers, and captive users. Compliance mechanisms include direct consumption, RECs, and buyout provisions. 
• Electricity Rules Amendment – Captive Generation (2026): Expands the definition of ownership (including subsidiaries 
and holding structures), facilitating greater participation in 
captive power projects. 
• Draft Policy Developments: Draft amendments to the Electricity Act, 2003 and the National Electricity Policy, 2026 
have been issued for stakeholder consultation, indicating 
continued policy evolution in the sector.
• RE Manufacturing Boost:  GST on renewable equipment 
reduced from 12% to 5%; launch of Renewable Energy 
Equipment Import Monitoring System (REEIMS); incentives 
for domestic battery manufacturing.
• Customs Duty Exemption: Union Budget 2026–27 extended 
customs duty exemption on imports for all nuclear power 
projects until 2035.
• Electricity (Amendment) Rules 2025:  Allowed integration 
of consumer-owned energy storage systems with the grid, boosting distributed flexibility.
NTPC - COMPANY PERFORMANCE AND STRATEGIC POSITIONING
NTPC’s Strategic Positioning in Global Context
As India advances towards its vision of becoming a Viksit Bharat 
by 2047, its electricity demand is projected to grow at 6–6.5% per annum, significantly higher than the global average of approximately 
2.8%. Sustaining this long-term economic growth will be critical, 
underpinned by rising industrialization, urbanization, digitalization, and improving standards of living, all of which are expected to drive 
strong growth in electricity demand. Concurrently, the push towards 
energy independence through electrification of mobility, industry, and cooling needs is set to further accelerate power consumption, 
positioning the sector for sustained high growth. 
Against this backdrop, NTPC is well placed to lead India’s energy 
transition while ensuring energy security and sustainable growth, 
demonstrated by its strong operational performance during the year, including a record capacity addition of 9.6 GW taking the 
overall capacity to 89+GW (including 0.75 GW PSP) and electricity 
generation exceeding 400 billion units for the second consecutive financial year, contributing to nearly 24% of the country’s total 
generation. The Company’s continued focus on scale, efficiency, 
and clean energy expansion shall enhance the resilience of its business model in view of ever-changing dynamics of the sector, 
while reinforcing its pivotal role in supporting India’s growth 
aspirations.Management Discussion & Analysis ReportManagement Discussion & Analysis Report

Fuel Sec urity
NTPC has adopted a robust and forward-looking strategy to ensure 
fuel security for its extensive fleet of thermal power plants. This strategy focuses on mitigating risks associated with fuel shortages, 
price fluctuations, and logistical challenges by enhancing domestic 
coal production, diversifying procurement sources, and eliminating imports. 
The company has secured 100% fuel tie-up for its thermal capacity 
through long-term Fuel Supply Agreements (FSAs) with coal 
companies (CIL & SCCL), with a total Annual Contracted Quantity (ACQ) of 256.92 MMT across the NTPC group. During FY 2025–26, ACQ materialization from coal companies stood at 84%. NTPC 
further strengthened its fuel security by sourcing 43.5 MMT of coal 
from its captive mines. 
NTPC has also procured domestic coal on FOR (Free on Rail) 
destination basis from commercial mines & surplus coal from captive blocks through competitive bidding. Thus, NTPC offset 
the shortfall from linked sources without procuring imported coal, 
thereby reducing the overall cost of power generation.
Captive Coal Mining
To strengthen fuel security, NTPC continues to expand its captive 
coal mining portfolio, with a target to increase production capacity from 91.6 MMTPA to 100 MMTPA and beyond.
To enhance operational focus, NTPC has consolidated its mining 
activities under its wholly owned subsidiary, NTPC Mining Limited (NML). With the transfer of Pakri Barwadih Coal mine on 01st April 2026, all the six coal mines have been transferred from NTPC 
to NML. While one mine – Badam- is under development, NML currently operates five mines - Pakri-Barwadih, Dulanga, Talaipalli, 
Chatti-Bariatu, and Kerandari, all of which have been declared commercial.
Coal production from the captive mines, including production from 
the Amelia mine operated by THDC India Limited, stood at 48.65 MMT during the year, 6.22% higher than the previous fiscal.
Operations from Badam mine are expected to commence in 
FY 2026–27, while progress continues on the Banhardih mine 
(PVUNL). NML has also secured its first commercial coal block, 
North-Dadhu (Eastern Part) with the mining plan approved, and 
development activities in progress.
In addition to coal, NML is actively pursuing diversification into 
critical minerals, supported by strategic collaborations with leading institutions and industry partners.
Through these initiatives, NTPC aims to build a resilient, cost-
effective domestic fuel supply base, while supporting long-term energy security and emerging transition requirements.
Power Trading (NVVN)
Durin g FY 2025-26, NTPC strengthened its diversified energy and 
sustainability portfolio through its subsidiary NVVN, delivering 
robust growth across power trading, renewable energy, waste-to-energy and carbon management businesses. Power trading 
volume increased by 13% to 46.38 BU, driven by strong growth 
in exchange-based and cross-border power trading, including addition of the Punatsangchu-II hydro project in Bhutan. The 
Company also expanded its renewable energy portfolio with over 227 MW of rooftop and ground-mounted solar projects under commissioning, construction and tendering stages. Significant 
progress was achieved in waste-to-energy projects at Varanasi, Noida, Gorakhpur, Bhopal and Hubballi-Dharwad, while battery 
energy storage projects and consultancy assignments further 
strengthened the clean energy portfolio. During the year, NVVN also enhanced its participation in emerging carbon markets, expanded 
gas trading operations, and implemented multiple digital initiatives 
for power exchange bidding, analytics and cross-border scheduling, reinforcing its focus on innovation, sustainability and integrated 
energy solutions.
Renewa ble Energy (NTPC Group)
NTPC continues to expand its capacity in line with India’s growth 
trajectory while advancing its commitment to energy transition and 
net-zero objectives. The Company has set an ambitious target of 
244 GW (and 6 GW PSP) installed capacity by 2037, including RE capacity targets of 60 GW by 2032 and 136 GW by 2037.
During FY 2025–26, NTPC achieved a key milestone by crossing 
10 GW of installed RE capacity, reaching 11.6 GW as on 31
st March 
2026, with ~15 GW under implementation and an additional ~6.4 
GW under tendering/award.
NTPC Green Energy Limited (NGEL) is spearheading the Company’s 
green initiatives, supported by strategic joint ventures incorporated 
with several states including Maharashtra, Rajasthan, Chhattisgarh, UP and Andhra Pradesh, facilitating faster capacity addition through 
improved access to land, grid connectivity, and approvals, reducing 
the dispatch risk.
NTPC Group’s RE portfolio comprises 56 operational projects, 
including key developments such as Khavda Solar Park (Gujarat), 
Nokh, and Bhadla-II (Rajasthan). Additionally, 46 projects (~15

The Company has signed MoUs with multiple states for developing

Green & Emerging Businesses
Green Hydrogen
A major milestone in NTPC’s energy security roadmap is setting up 
of a 1,200-acre green hydrogen hub at Pudimadaka, Andhra Pradesh 
with the foundation stone laid by the Hon’ble Prime Minister. Key 
infrastructure work is currently underway, alongside pilot projects for Green Ethanol (10 TPD), Sustainable Aviation Fuel (SAF) (6 TPD) and Green Urea (150 TPD). Strategically located near seacoast, this hub is poised to become a catalyst for India’s hydrogen economy. 
With the facilities for production of green hydrogen, green ammonia, 
e-methanol, SAF etc., the project is expected to utilise 7 GW of RE-RTC in its final phase, exporting up to 2.5 MMTPA of green hydrogen 
derivatives. Apart from this mega project, several unique initiatives 
have been taken up by NTPC in the green hydrogen space including commissioning of Green hydrogen-PNG blending project at Kawas, 
achieving blending of 8% vol/vol; commissioning of world’s highest-
altitude Green Hydrogen Fuelling station Leh, Ladakh leading to first commercial operation of Hydrogen FCEV buses in India (at Leh); 
commissioning India’s largest Green Hydrogen Fuelling Station 
in Greater NOIDA(UP) for plying of 5 Hydrogen FCEVs in intercity mode; and partnering with the Indian Army to establish a Solar 
Hydrogen-based Microgrid at Chushul, Ladakh, which is also the 
world’s highest-altitude green hydrogen project located at 4400 m above Mean Sea Level. NTPC has also become the first CPSE to set 
up a Green Ammonia project (of 70,000 TPA capacity) won under 
the ambit of National Green Hydrogen Mission.
Battery Energy Storage (BESS)
Ministry of Power (MoP) vide letter dated 09.06.2025 has allocated 
5 GWh Battery Energy Storage System (BESS) capacity to be 
installed at various NTPC power stations for development under the 
VGF scheme supported through Power System Development Fund (PSDF) with a viability Gap Funding (VGF) of ₹18 lakh/MWh. NTPC 
has identified 16 thermal power projects for development of “BESS 
projects” with an aggregate capacity of 5 GWh (15 BESS projects of cumulative 4.7 GWh at NTPC stations and 1 project of 0.3 GWh at 
NTECL Vallur) which are under various stages of implementation. 
Ministry of Power vide letter dated 12.01.2026 has sanctioned VGF grant of ₹900 crore for implementation of these projects.
Pumped Storage
NTPC Group vide THDC’s Tehri Pumped Storage Project got its first 
commercial PSP capacity with three units of 250 MW each being 
commissioned in FY 2025-26 and the fourth and last unit of 250 MW being commissioned on 12
th April 2026. NTPC Group has an 
elaborate PSP portfolio of over 18 GW with 4,800 MW capacity 
allocated from NTPC to its group companies NTECL, THDC and 
NEEPCO. Additionally, THDC (10,110 MW) and NEEPCO (2,100 MW) have direct allocation of PSPs under various stages of execution.

SWOT Analysis — NTPC Group
The following matrix presents a structured assessment of NTPC’s internal capabilities and the external environment shaping its strategic 
choices:Strengths
NTPC continues to maintain its leadership position as India’s 
largest integrated power utility, with a group installed capacity 
exceeding 89 GW. During FY26, the Company achieved a record capacity addition of 9,618 MW, reflecting strong project execution 
capabilities. Operational performance remains robust, with coal-
based stations operating at a Plant Load Factor (PLF) of ~72%, 
higher than the national average of ~65.5%.
The Company has developed a diversified portfolio spanning 
thermal, hydro, renewable energy, nuclear, and emerging areas 
such as green hydrogen, enabling it to effectively participate in the 
evolving energy landscape. Even as NTPC continues to undertake 
one of the sector’s largest capital expenditure programmes, it 
improved its debt-equity ratio from 1.15x in FY25 to 1.09x in FY26, 
reflecting prudent leverage management, stronger balance sheet 
resilience, and greater headroom to access low-cost debt for the 
upcoming growth cycle.
The steady growth in PAT and net worth further underscores 
the Company’s strong financial discipline along with sustained 
operating cash flows, and improved debt service coverage and 
interest coverage ratios. Commercial performance remains strong with 100% billing realisation and secured payment mechanisms 
under tripartite agreements. Additionally, the Company has 
demonstrated sustained improvement in ESG performance and 
sustainability initiatives, as evidenced by significant upgrades in its 
ratings from several reputed agencies.
Weaknesses
The increasing penetration of renewable energy has led to a 
decline in coal PLF (down by ~5 percentage points), impacting utilisation levels of thermal assets. Gas-based capacity continues 
to remain underutilised, primarily due to fuel availability and pricing 
constraints.
Opportunities
India’s electricity demand is expected to grow at 6–6.5% per 
annum, driven by increased electrification, digitalisation, electric 
mobility, and data centre expansion, providing significant growth 
opportunities. The Government’s target of achieving 500 GW of 
non-fossil capacity by 2030 necessitates accelerated renewable 
capacity addition, positioning NTPC to expand its clean energy 
portfolio.
Policy support for nuclear expansion for reaching capacity of 100 
GW by 2047, including enabling provisions for private participation, offers long-term diversification opportunities. The Company is also 
well placed to leverage emerging areas such as green hydrogen, 
green ammonia, and sustainable aviation fuel (SAF), including export-oriented initiatives.
Additionally, opportunities exist in carbon markets, with NTPC 
having already generated carbon credits, and in the commercial and industrial (C&I) segment through virtual power purchase 
agreements (VPPAs) and open access mechanisms.
Threats 
The increasing share of renewable energy (RE) introduces 
operational challenges, including the “duck curve” effect, characterised by periods of surplus solar generation and steep 
ramping requirements for thermal capacities. Higher penetration 
of variable RE increases grid integration complexity, requiring enhanced flexibility, storage solutions, and system balancing 
capabilities. While this provides an opportunity for the NTPC’s 
capacities to operate as peaking capacities, the rate of increase in peak demand may surpass the rate of growth of energy demand 
leading to sharper peaks owing to cooling load, data centre demand 
and EV demand expansion, which maybe difficult for coal plants to serve effectively. Further, a downward trend in the BESS tariffs 
is also making solar + BESS more attractive to meet the non-solar 
hours peaking requirement, competing with new thermal capacities. However, a level of mitigation of the risk due to flexible operation 
of coal-based capacities is provided by CERC’s tariff regulations 
offering higher percentage of ROE for higher ramp rate capability. With higher projections of thermal capacities under National 
Generation Adequacy Plan 2026, up to 315 GW by 2035-36, CEA 
has given strong indications of the continued importance of coal-based capacities in maintaining reliability of the grid whether by 
way of base-load generation, ramping capability or reserve peaking 
provisions.
For the high-growth plans of RE capacity addition by NTPC Group, 
the threat is in form of excess solar supply during day-time compressing market prices and causing high price volatility through 
the day, thus eroding the margins in an already competitive play 
space. Transmission bottlenecks are exacerbating the curtailment of RE supply from new and upcoming projects leading to revenue 
loss.
CAPACITY TARGETSThe Company revised its total capacity target upward to 149 GW by 
2032 and 244 GW by 2037, from the earlier 130 GW by 2032. This reflects the government’s accelerated 500 GW non-fossil target 
and India’s rising power demand trajectory. By 2032, the fuel mix 
will comprise 60 GW of renewables, ~84 GW of thermal (all future additions via ultra-supercritical technology), and a growing nuclear 
portfolio.Management Discussion & Analysis ReportManagement Discussion & Analysis Report

RESEARCH AND DEVELOPMENT
NTPC continues to strengthen its technological leadership through 
focused research and innovation. Its R&D centre, NETRA (NTPC 
Energy Technology Research Alliance), drives development and 
deployment of advanced technologies to address key sectoral challenges while enabling new business opportunities.
The Company is actively pursuing initiatives in carbon capture, 
energy storage, green hydrogen, coal gasification, and ash 
utilisation, aligned with its energy transition strategy.
Key R & D Initiatives:
• Carbon Capture, Utilisation & Storage (CCUS): Projects 
across capture, utilisation, and storage, including 6,000 TPA 
commissioned, 22,500 TPA under execution, and 100,000 TPA 
planned. Downstream applications include CO2-to-ethanol, 
methanol, urea, and sustainable aviation fuel (SAF), along with CO
2 transport and geological storage studies. 
• Ener gy Storage: Development of advanced storage solutions, 
including VRFB systems, CO2-based closed Brayton cycle 
storage, and thermal energy storage applications. 
• Gr een Hydrogen: Pilot-scale projects including seawater-
based hydrogen production and plasma gasification-based 
hydrogen systems. 
• Coal Gasification: Development of a 5 lakh TPA synthetic 
natural gas (SNG) project at Talaipalli, with technology selection and design studies in progress. 
• Ash Utilisation: Scaling of value-added applications such as fly 
ash-based bricks and aggregates. Through these initiatives, NTPC is building capabilities in next-
generation technologies to support decarbonisation, resource 
efficiency, and future energy solutions.

Revenue From Operations 
Revenue from operations primarily comprises of variable charges 
for electricity generation and fixed (capacity) charges towards recovery of fixed costs. Together, these two components constitute more than 95% of revenue from operations in both the financial years & the same have been accounted for in line with the CERC tariff regulations 2024 as amended from time to time.
Revenue from operations decreased by 2.67 % from ₹1,70,037.37 
crore in FY 2024-25 to ₹1,65,493.74 crore in FY 2025-26, mainly 
due to Lower Energy Sent Out (ESO) by 19.844 BU from 347.292 
BU in FY  2024 25 to 327.448 BU in FY 2025-26(due to lower power 
demand). This is partly offset by commissioning of new capacities 
during the years, favourable tariff orders & 2nd amendment to 
CERC tariff regulations.  (Refer note 38 at page 263)
PLF of Coal stations in FY 2025-26 was 72.04% against rest of India coal PLF of 63.20% underscoring the Company’s strong operational 
performance and maintenance capabilities.

FY 2024-25 to ₹10,442.18 Crore in FY 2025-26, mainly due to repayment of loans and a reduction in rate of borrowings resulting 
from proactive restructuring and refinancing of loans. The weighted 
average rate of borrowings has decreased from 6.61% in FY 2024-25 to 5.98% in FY 2025-26.  
(Refer note 42 at page 266)
Depreciation 
Depreciation expense increased by 6.48% from ₹15055.84 
Crore in FY 2024-25 to ₹16,030.85 Crore in FY 2025-26, due to commissioning of additional capacity and capital expenditure on 
existing stations. 
(Refer note 43 at page 267)
Other Expenses 
Other expenses mainly comprise of repair & maintenance 
expense, Exchange rate variation (ERV), Station overheads & Ash 
transportation expenses. Other expenses increased by 23.93% 
from ₹18,111.60 Crore to ₹22,445.63 Crore, mainly on account of unfavourable exchange rate variation, for which regulatory income has been created to the extent allowable under CERC tariff regulations and provision for impairment of investment of group 
companies. 
(Refer note 44 at page 268)
EBITDA 
EBITDA (Including regulatory adjustments) increased by 4.84%  
from ₹49,785.05 crore in FY 2024-25 to Rs 52,195.07 Crore 
in FY 2025-26, primarily on account of higher revenue from 
commissioning of new capacities during the years, favourable 
tariff orders & the 2nd amendment to CERC tariff regulations partly 
offset by higher provisions for impairment on investment in group companies and tariff adjustment etc.
Profit after tax (PAT) Profit after tax increased by 17.88% from ₹19,649.41 Crore in FY 
2024-25 to ₹23,162.22 Crore for FY 2025-26. The improvement 
was primarily driven by higher regulated equity on account of commissioning of additional capacity and capital expenditure in existing stations, higher dividend income from group companies, 
favourable tariff orders & impact of 2nd amendment to CERC tariff 
regulations.
Return on Net Worth (RONW) 
Return on net worth increas
ed from 12.61% in FY  2024 25 to 13.77% 
in FY  2025 26, reflecting higher profitability, partly moderated by an 
increase in net worth on account of retained earnings.Key Ratios

Dividend
The Board of Directors has recommended a final dividend of 
₹3.50 per equity share for FY  2025 26, subject to approval of the members at the ensuing Annual General Meeting. If approved,  
the total dividend for the year would amount to ₹9.00 per equity 
share, representing an increase of approximately 7.78% over 
FY 2024-25. 
The Company continues to maintain a healthy dividend payout 
ratio in the range of about 35-40%, reflecting its balanced approach 
towards rewarding shareholders while retaining adequate earnings 
to support future growth and capital requirements.
Debtors turnover declined due to higher trade receivables and lower revenue from operations, while inventory turnover declined marginally 
due to change in inventory levels and revenue from operations. Interest coverage strengthened on account of higher operating profitability, 
and current ratio marginally moderated from 0.96 in the previous year to 0.94 during the current year, primarily reflecting a relatively higher increase in current liabilities vis-à-vis current assets. However, the ratio continues to remain below unity, indicating reliance on efficient 
working capital management, strong operating cash flows, and access to short-term funding lines to meet near-term obligations.
The debt–equity ratio declined, indicating strengthening of the capital structure through higher internal accruals. Operating and net profit 
margins improved during the year, driven by Capacity additions, favourable tariff orders & 2
nd amendment to CERC tariff regulations, 
consistent with the regulated nature of the Company’s operations.

The Company has established robust internal control systems 
comprising policies, procedures and control frameworks designed to enhance operational efficiency, ensure adherence to policies, and 
support smooth and effective business processes. The internal control systems are commensurate with the size and nature of 
the Company’s operations and are supported by an independent 
Internal Audit Department, which conducts audits across business 
processes on a continuous basis. In accordance with section  143(3)
(i) of the Companies Ac t, 2013, the Statutory Auditors issue a 
separate report on the adequacy and operating effectiveness of 
internal financial controls over financial reporting, which forms 
part of the Standalone and Consolidated Financial Statements. The Audit Committee reviews the financial statements and audit  observations in consultation with the Internal and Statutory Auditors 
before recommending the same to the Board for approval

Corporate Governance refers to adoption of sound management 
practices, compliance with applicable laws, and adherence 
to ethical standards to achieve the Company’s objectives, 
enhancing stakeholder value, and fulfilling social responsibilities. It  
encompasses the relationships among various stakeholders, such 
as shareholders, management, employees, customers, suppliers 
and the community at large. The objective of corporate governance is to manage the business to maximise long-term value, while 
ensuring the protection of stakeholders’ interests.
This report is prepared in accordance with the provisions of SEBI 
(Listing Obligations and Disclosure Requirements) Regulations, 2015 
(‘Listing Regulations’) and the Guidelines on Corporate Governance for Central Public Sector Enterprises, 2010 (‘CG Guidelines’) 
issued by the Department of Public Enterprises (‘DPE’), Ministry of 
Finance, Government of India, highlighted corporate governance methodology at NTPC Limited (‘NTPC’/ ‘the Company’).
1. N TPC’s Corporate Governance Philosophy
OUR CORPORATE GOVERNANCE PHILOSOPHY
“As a good corporate governance citizen, our company is committed to sound corporate practices based on 
conscience, openness, fairness, professionalism and 
accountability besides building confidence in its various stakeholders, thereby paving the way for the long term 
success. ”
 The Company ’s philosophy on corporate governance oversees 
business strategies and ensures fiscal accountability, 
ethical corporate behaviour and fairness to all stakeholders 
comprising investors, Employees, customers, regulators, 
suppliers and the society at large. Our dedicated initiatives in fostering and maintaining the highest standards of governance 
are presented in this report.
2. Bo ard of Directors
 The Board of Directors, as the apex body constituted by 
shareholders, provides strategic direction and leadership to 
the Company and oversees management policies and their 
effectiveness, with a focus on long-term shareholder and 
stakeholder interests. It is responsible for driving economy, efficiency, and effectiveness in operations, while ensuring 
value creation and sustainable growth. The Board discharges its functions in accordance with the Companies Act, 2013 
(‘the Act’), Listing Regulations, the Company’s Memorandum and Articles of Association, Maharatna Guidelines & CG 
Guidelines issued by DPE, and other applicable directions of 
the Government of India.
2.1  Co mposition of Board
 N TPC is a Government Company under Section 2(45) of the 
Act and, according to its Articles of Association, all Directors are appointed by the President of India. The approved Board 
composition included six (6) Functional Directors (including the Chairman & Managing Director), two (2) Government 
Nominee Directors, and eight (8) Independent Directors—one (1) of whom is required to be a woman in accordance with Listing Regulations. However, as on 31
st March 2026, the Board 
comprised six (6) Functional Directors, two (2) Government 
Nominee Directors, and only five (5) Independent Directors 
including one (1) woman Independent Director. During FY 2025–26, numbers of Independent Directors were less 
than half of the Board. Further, the mandates regarding the 
presence of a woman independent director and at least 50% non-executive directors were not fulfilled until 18
th May 2025. 
NTPC has requested the Administrative Ministry i.e. Ministry 
of Power (‘MoP’) for appointments of the necessary number of 
independent and non-executive directors.
 The present strength of the Board reflects judicious mix of 
professionalism, competence and sound knowledge which enables the Board to provide effective leadership to the 
Company.
2.1.1 Key skills, expertise, competencies of the Board of Directors
 The Board comprises qualified members possessing the 
necessary skills, competence and expertise to effectively 
contribute to Board and Committee deliberations. The Board 
of Directors had approved the job description, qualifications 
and experience requirements for Board-level positions. The candidates for the position of Functional Director on the Board 
of the Company are selected by the Public Enterprise Selection 
Board. 
 The Boar d of Directors had also decided that Independent 
Directors nominated by the Government of India are expected to possess expertise in diverse fields such as Technical/

d) T ransfer of Unclaimed Amount of Dividend to Investor Education & Protection Fund (IEPF)
 In accor dance with Section 124(5) of the Act read with Investor Education and Protection Fund Authority (Accounting, Audit, 
Transfer and Refund) Rules, 2016, (“IEPF Rules, 2016”), the Company transferred unclaimed dividend amounts aggregating 
to ₹525.95 lakh to the Investor Education and Protection Fund (IEPF) during FY 2025-26. The amount transferred comprised  
₹105.03 lakh towards Interim Dividend for FY 2017-18, ₹115.65 lakh towards Final Dividend for FY 2017-18, ₹153.79 lakh towards Interim Dividend for FY 2018-19, ₹56.30 lakh towards Final Dividend for FY 2024-25, ₹46.01 lakh towards First Interim Dividend for FY 2025-26 and ₹49.17 lakh towards Second Interim Dividend for FY 2025-26. In compliance with the aforesaid provisions, the 
Company has uploaded on its website the details of shareholders containing information such as name, address, amount due 
for transfer to IEPF and the due date of such transfer. Further, the Company has been issuing notices in newspapers from time to time and taking other prescribed measures to draw the attention of shareholders and invite them to claim their unpaid and 
unclaimed dividend before the amounts become due for transfer to the IEPF.
e) T ransfer of Shares to IEPF
 Pursuant to the provisions of Section 124(6) of the Act, 2013 read with the IEPF Rules, 2016, all shares in respect of which dividend 
has remained unpaid or unclaimed for a continuous period of seven consecutive years or more are required to be transferred to 
the Demat Account of the IEPF Authority. Accordingly, during FY 2025-26, the Company transferred 3,01,016 equity shares to the 
Demat Account of the IEPF Authority maintained with CDSL, in compliance with the provisions of Section 124(6) of the Act, the 
IEPF Rules and the circulars/notifications issued by the Ministry of Corporate Affairs from time to time.
 The details of shareholders whose shares have been transferred to the IEPF Authority are available on the Company’s website. 
Shareholders may access the details at https://ntpc.co.in/iepf-details/iepf-account  and verify their records. Such shareholders 
may claim their shares and the corresponding benefits, if any, from the IEPF Authority by following the procedure prescribed under 
the Act and the IEPF Rules.f) Cla im from IEPF Account
 Any person whose shares, unclaimed dividend, matured deposits, matured debentures, application money due for refund, or 
interest thereon, sale proceeds of fractional share etc. has been transferred to the IEPF, may claim the shares under provision to 
sub-section (6) of section 124 or apply for refund under clause (a) of sub-section (3) of section 125 of the Act as the case may be, 
by submitting an online application in Form IEPF-5 to the IEPF Authority in accordance with the prescribed procedure.
 The detailed procedure regarding claiming shares and/or refund of amounts from the IEPF Authority is available on the Company’s 
website at the following link: https://ntpc.co.in/iepf-account/procedure-claiming-dividend-shares-iepf-authority

8.8 Sha re Transfer System
As mandated by SEBI, securities of the Company can be transferred/traded only in dematerialised form. Shareholders holding shares in physical form are advised to avail the facility of dematerialisation. Notices, in this regard, have been hosted on the website of 
the Company, informing the shareholders to hold the shares in dematerialised form. Form ISR-4 (for physical shareholders) is also 
available on the website of the Company. The documents are hosted on https://ntpc.co.in/investor/investor-updates/forms-investors 
Pursuant to various SEBI Circulars, the Company, vide its various communications viz. emails/ letters/ AGM Notice/ newspaper 
advertisements, has informed the shareholders to update their PAN, Nomination, Contact details, Bank A/c details and Specimen signature etc. for their corresponding folio numbers in the record of Depository Participant(s). List of documents is also hosted on 
https://ntpc.co.in/investor-updates/important-notices-security-holders
Special window for transfer and dematerialization of physical securities
Pursuant to the SEBI Circular dated 30
th January 2026, a special window has been provided from 5th February 2026 to 4th February 2027 
for transfer and dematerialization of physical securities sold or purchased prior to 1st April 2019, where transfer requests were earlier 
rejected, returned, or remained unattended due to documentation or procedural deficiencies. Such securities, upon transfer, shall be 
credited only in demat mode and will remain under lock-in for one year from the date of transfer registration, during which they cannot 
be transferred, pledged, or lien-marked.In order to create awareness amongst shareholders, the Company has been issuing bi-monthly advertisements in newspapers and has also hosted the relevant Circular on the Company’s website.

A. CO NSERVATION OF ENERGY:
a) Ene rgy conservation measures taken:
 Som e of the key energy conservation measures implemented 
during the FY 2025-26 in various areas are as under:
i. ENERGY AUDITS
 In 2025-26, Mandatory Energy Audits were conducted at 07 
stations in accordance with BEE regulations. All other NTPC 
stations have carried out Auxiliary Power Consumption Energy 
Audits, and 09 stations have conducted water audits as per planned schedule. 
ii. AUXILIARY POWER CONSUMPTION
 Som e of the actions undertaken to reduce auxiliary power 
consumption at various stations are:
-  Replacement of inefficient Boiler Feed Pump (BFP) 
cartridges based on high Specific Energy Consumption 
(SEC). 
-  Replacement of mill internal s based upon SEC of mills 
-  Replacement of tube mill lin ers. 
-  Replacement of Ash Slurry Pumps with energy-efficient 
pumps. 
-  Optimisatio n of Bottom ash deashing process 
-  Reg ular online and offline compressor washing in gas 
turbines 
-  Replacement of ceiling fans with Brushless DC (BLDC) 
fans. 
-  Inst allation of grid-connected rooftop solar PV systems. 
-  Application of energy-efficient coatings on the internals of 
cooling water and other large water pumps. 
-  Replacement of left-over conventional lighting by LED 
fittings. 
-  Replacement of existing motors with energy-efficient 
motors. 
-  Replacement of old compressors with screw compressors. -  Optimizatio n of the numbers of running major equipment 
such as BFPs, CEPs, mills, CW pumps, and CT fans during extended periods of partial loading. 
-  Ex cess O2 optimisation at Part Load 
-  APH  Seal Setting 
- Inst allation in VFD in L T drives as LDO pumps, Mill feeders 
iii. NET ZERO ENERGY TOWNSHIPS AND OFFICES
 N TPC has developed a roadmap to achieve Net Zero for its 
Townships and Offices. NTPC townships at Kudgi, Solapur and offices at NETRA, and WR-II HQ at Raipur have been declared 
net zero energy establishments. 
iv. LIGHTING 
 Replacement of conventional lighting with LEDs wherever 
balance in various areas, including the main plant, off-sites, 
office buildings, street lighting and common facilities of the 
station and township, and residential units within the township 
were continued during the year. 
v. HEAT ENERGY

stations are:
- Replacement of Cooling Tower (CT) fill pack & CT R&M.

- TDBFP car tridge replacement 
- Boiler modifications for enhancing steam parameters and 
efficiency.
- Modification of cooling tower water nozzles to ensure 
proper water distribution.

1B.  Scientific Ser vices Support to Power Stations:
 NE TRA provides continuous, specialized scientific services 
to NTPC stations and other power utilities to enhance reliability, safety, and efficiency across plant operations. 
Its key contributions include advanced health assessment 
and residual life evaluation of critical components such as boilers, turbines, and transformers using state-of-the-art 
non-destructive evaluation (NDE) techniques and in-house 
developed robotic inspection systems. NETRA also conducts detailed root cause analysis of equipment failures, develops 
chemical solutions for high-cycle cooling water treatment to 
optimize water usage, and provides corrosion monitoring and control strategies. The center supports condition monitoring 
of transformers, superheater tubes, lubricating oils, and resins, 
ensuring early detection of faults and extending equipment life. NETRA’s advanced coal and ash characterization enables 
better fuel management, while its technical support for 
biomass and municipal solid waste (MSW) co-firing promotes cleaner energy solutions. By reducing reliance on OEMs for 
complex diagnostics, NETRA’s scientific services significantly 
contribute to plant efficiency, cost optimization, and sustainable operations. Details of specific projects can be accessed from 
NETRA page at NTPC’s website at https://www.ntpc.co.in/
about-us/corporate-functions/netra/about-netra

Annual Report on CSR  Activities
1. A brief outline of  the Company’s CSR policy
NTPC Limited, India’s largest energy conglomerate, has been 
at the forefront of driving the country’s energy needs while also 
emphasizing sustainable development and corporate social 
responsibility (CSR). The NTPC CSR Policy, revised in 2022, is 
a testament to the company’s commitment in creating value 
for both business and society. This policy aligns with NTPC’s 
vision to be the World’s Leading Power Company, accelerating 
India’s Growth & Energy Transition, while its mission focuses 
on providing reliable power and energy transition solutions 
in an economical, efficient and environment-friendly manner, driven by innovation and agility. These guiding statements 
underline NTPC’s commitment to not only power generation 
but also sustainable and impactful growth. The CSR policy is 
an extension of this vision.
The policy emphasizes focusing on four main areas: education, 
water, health, and sanitation. Further, other thematic areas like 
sports, women empowerment, vocational skill development 
etc. are also given due importance in the policy framework. 
To bring maximum value to society, the activities are 
selected based on need assessment surveys, inputs from 
various stakeholders, and alignment with Schedule VII of the 
Companies Act. It advocates for outcome-centric projects 
monitored for their impact and opportunities for improvement, thereby ensuring effective communication with stakeholders 
to instil confidence.
The policy is applicable across all NTPC stations in India, 
encompassing the formulation, implementation, monitoring, evaluation, documentation, and reporting of CSR activities 
undertaken by NTPC throughout the country. This ensures 
a unified and standardized approach to CSR across the 
organization.
NTPC’s CSR efforts are primarily focusing on the local area 
or immediate vicinities of its stations and locations. NTPC 
allocates fund in a defined ratio for local area and outside, 
including projects of national importance. The CSR committee 
has the authority to approve projects beyond this ratio based 
on specific requirements, such as natural calamities or key community needs.The core principles that guide NTPC’s CSR activities are:

 Self-Suppor ted and Sustainable: Projects are designed 
for long-term viability, ensuring that communities can 
maintain the assets and systems created even after the 
project’s completion.
 Low Cost - High Impact: The focus is on adopting cost-
efficient and impactful solutions.
 Long-Lasting and Enduring: Priority is given to projects 
that offer sustainable and lasting benefits to the 
community.
 Str ategic Alignment to Core Business: CSR activities 
are aligned with NTPC’s strengths and capabilities to leverage the company’s core competencies.

 Measur ement and Feedback-Based Outcomes: All 
projects have defined measures for assessing their impact, with third-party assessments for high-impact 
projects to ensure objective evaluation and feedback.
NTPC’s CSR activities are governed by a board-level CSR 
Committee comprising at least three directors, including one independent director. The governance structure includes a 
three-tier system at corporate, regional, and station levels, 
responsible for planning, implementation, monitoring, and 
reporting on CSR projects.
At the Corporate Level, responsibilities include policy 
formulation, strategic project selection, budget planning, 
monitoring, and capability development of CSR professionals. 
The Regional Level focuses on coordination and monitoring 
of state or region-level activities, while the Station Level 
handles project selection (regular), implementation, budget 
planning, and management information systems (MIS). 
The effectiveness of CSR projects is assessed through 
internal and external evaluations, periodic audits, and impact assessments.
The CSR annual action plans and budgets are proposed 
by stations, regions, and corporate CSR departments, 
consoli dated, and approved by the CSR Committee and the 
Board.Annual Report on C SR ActivitiesAnnexure to Directors’ Report

4. Pr ovide the executive summary along with web link(s) of Impact Assessment of CSR projects carried out in 
pursuance of sub-rule (3) of rule 8 of the Companies (Corporate Social responsibility Policy) Rules, 2014: 
NTPC’s CSR initiatives are guided by its commitment to creating sustainable and inclusive development in the communities surrounding 
its operations. The Company’s CSR strategy focuses on improving quality of life through interventions in education, healthcare, 
skill development, environmental sustainability, rural development, women empowerment, drinking water, sanitation, and livelihood 
enhancement. These initiatives are implemented in alignment with the Company’s CSR Policy and national development priorities.
As part of its commitment to ensuring accountability and measuring the effectiveness of its CSR interventions, NTPC undertook 
impact assessments of CSR projects in accordance with the requirements of the Companies Act, 2013 and the Companies (Corporate 
Social Responsibility Policy) Rules, 2014, as amended.
The impact assessment studies were carried out by an independent external agency using a comprehensive methodology that 
included desk reviews, field visits, stakeholder consultations, beneficiary surveys, focused group discussions, and in-depth interviews. Information collected from both primary and secondary sources was analysed to assess the relevance, effectiveness, efficiency, 
coherence, sustainability, and long-term impact of the interventions on the target communities.
 The assessment indicate that the projects have generated significant socio-economic benefits across diverse thematic areas, including 
healthcare, education, girl child empowerment, and sports promotion. The interventions contributed to strengthening healthcare 
infrastructure, improving access to specialized medical services, enhancing educational infrastructure and learning environments, 
supporting quality education, promoting sports development, and empowering adolescent girls through holistic development initiatives. Ov erall, these projects have positively impacted the quality of life of beneficiaries and contributed to sustainable community 
development.

With a view to focus on its role a s a socially responsible and 
socially conscious organization, NTPC has endeavoured to take 
responsibility for adequate representation of physically challenged 
persons in its workforce. With this in view, total of 45 PwBD were 
recruited during the year 2025. As on 1st January 2026, 535 (3.14%) 
PwBD (90 with blindness and low vision, 112 with deaf and hard of hearing, 331 with locomotor disabilities, 1 with autism/ intellectual 
disability and 1 with multiple disability) are on the rolls of the 
company. Reservation has been provided as per rules/policy. Some 
of the other initiatives taken for the welfare of PwBD over the years 
by NTPC are as under:
– In complian ce with The Rights of Persons with Disabilities Act 
(RPwD) 2016, NTPC has in place Equal Opportunity Policy.
– Add itional benefit of 4(four) days in the form of Special Casual 
leave in a calendar year for specific requirements relating to 
the disability of the employee has been provided to PwBD.
– T ravelling Allowance in respect of Attendant/Escort for 
accompanying an Employee with Disabilities on travel during Tour/Training.
– Liaison Officer (PwBD) and Grievance Redressal Officer have 
been nominated at all Projects/ Stations/ Regions.
– F or individual needs of the VH employees, screen reading 
software and Braille shorthand machines are made available by the Projects. A website has been made DAP (Differently 
abled Persons) friendly, particularly for Low Vision Employees.
– Changes in the existing building have been/are being made 
to provide barrier free access to differently abled. Ramps 
have also been provided for unhampered movement of wheel 
chairs.
– A t most of the NTPC Projects, wherever houses are located in 
multi-storied structures, allotments to PwBD has been made 
on the ground floor. Wherever required, gates/ door of the 
quarter has been widened.– N TPC Medial Attendance and Treatment (MAT) rules provide 
facility for reimbursement towards purchase/replacement of 
artificial limbs/appliances for self and/or eligible dependent 
family members and reimbursement towards Low Vision Aids 
for employees and their dependents and reimbursement of 
Hearing Aid to Employees and dependents of employees who 
are Hearing Impaired.
– Medical camps have been organized in various projects of 
NTPC for treatment and distribution of aids like artificial limbs, 
tricycles, wheelchairs, calipers etc.
– Shops ha ve been allotted in NTPC Township to DAP so that 
they may earn their livelihood.
– Reg ular interactive meetings are being organized with PwBD.
– In or der to encourage and motivate children and youth from 
neighbourhood villages of NTPC Projects/Stations for higher 
studies, NTPC has in place ‘NTPC Utkarsh’-Merit Scholarship 
under “NTPC Foundation” for students (including Physically 
Challenged) from the neighbourhood of its projects/ 
stations. The scheme benefits students from neighbourhood 
communities pursuing X, XII, ITI, BE/B.Tech and MBBS studies.
– In the recruitment process, percentage of marks to be attained 
in the required qualification is relaxed to a lesser percentage in case of SC/ST/PwBD candidates. Further, in case of written 
test and interview, 25% relaxation in marks of the qualifying 
marks of General Candidates is allowed to candidates 
belonging to SC/ST/OBC/PwBD categories.
– The minimum performance level marks for promotions 
(in workman categories) within the cluster is relaxed by 3 
marks in case of employees belonging to SC/ ST/ Physically 
Challenged categ ory.Annexure-VIII to Directors’ Report

Government of India (GoI) Memorandum of Understanding (MoU)  
2025-26 – Achievements
The GoI MoU is a performance agreement executed between the 
management of CPSEs and the Government of India. It is a major 
policy initiative of the Government of India to undertake a structured 
evaluation and drive improvements in the overall performance of CPSEs.
The GoI MoU for FY 2025-26 was signed between the Ministry of 
Power and NTPC on a group basis. During the year, your Company 
delivered a resilient performance across major parameters. The 
key achievements against the targets of the MoU 2025-26 are as follows:
Power Generation:  Your Company achieved a total power 
generation of 3,98,073 Million Units (MUs) during the year (including 
subsidiaries). The performance during the year was impacted by 
relatively subdued power demand in coal power stations; however, 
the Company maintained high levels of operational reliability across its diversified portfolio comprising thermal, hydro, and renewable 
energy assets.
Revenue from Operations:  Your Company achieved Revenue from 
Operations of ₹1,87,385 crore during the financial year. The revenue 
performance reflects the impact of moderated generation levels, while continuing to demonstrate stability supported by long-term 
power purchase agreements and regulated returns.
Financial Strength and Ratios:  Your Company continues to 
maintain strong financial discipline and a robust balance sheet, 
characterised by prudent capital management, healthy cash flows, 
and comfortable leverage levels. The Company demonstrated healthy profitability and strong credit fundamentals, enabling 
access to funds at competitive rates in domestic as well as 
international markets.
Key financial ratios achieved under the GoI MoU framework are as 
follows:

accrual basis.

of Goods & Services worth ₹20,864 crore through the Government e-Marketplace (GeM) portal (including subsidiaries), representing

This reflects strong adherence to procurement best practices, with

Digitalisation of process- Contractor safety assessment:

evidence-based decision-making, including contract

Management Reply on the Observations  
Provided  in Secretarial Audit Report
Observations Management’s Comments 
(a)  The Company was not in compliance with the requirements 
of the second proviso to Section 149(1) and Section 149(4) 
of the Companies Act, 2013, read with Regulation 17(1)(a) of 
the SEBI (Listing Obligations and Disclosure Requirements) 
Regulations, 2015, up to 18.05.2025. Further, during the 
financial year 2025–26, the Company was not in compliance 
with Regulation 17(1)(b) and Regulation 17(1E) of the SEBI (LODR) Regulations, 2015, as well as Clause 3.1.4 of the 
Department of Public Enterprises (DPE) Guidelines on 
Corporate Governance.NTPC Limited is a Government Company and as per the Articles 
of Association of the Company, the power to appoint or remove 
Directors on the Board of NTPC vests with the President of India 
through its administrative ministry i.e. Ministry of Power (MoP). 
Pursuant to the orders of MoP dated 16
th April 2025 and 15th May 
2025, the Company has appointed one Independent Director on  
17th April 2025, two Independent Directors on 16th May 2025 and 
further, two Independent Directors on 19th May 2025 (Including one 
Woman Independent Director). Thus, Company has complied with 
the provisions of one woman director (including ID) w.e.f. 19th May 
2025 and 50% non-executive directors w.e.f. 16th May 2025.
However, with regard to compliance with Regulation 17(1)(b) of 
the SEBI (LODR) Regulations, 2015, i.e. at least half of the Board 
of Directors shall comprise Independent Directors, the Board 
composition remained non-compliance during FY 2025-26. The 
matter has been consistently taken up with MOP for appointment of the requisite number of Independent Directors.
(b)  The Compa ny was not in compliance with the provisions of 
Regulations 18(1)(d), 19(1)(b), 19(2), 20(2A), and 21(2) of the 
SEBI (LODR) Regulations, 2015 up to 16.04.2025. Further, non-
compliance with Regulation 18(1)(b), Section 177(2) of the 
Companies Act, 2013 and Clause 4.1 of the DPE Guidelines on Corporate Governance up to 15.05.2025 and Regulation 
19(1)(c), Section 178(1) of the Companies Act, 2013 and 
Clause 5.1 of the DPE Guidelines on Corporate Governance up to 23.05.2025. Due to non-appointment of requisite number of Independent Directors, the Company remained non-compliance for certain period as mentioned under the observations. With the appointment 
of Independent Directors on the Board, the sub-committees of the 
Board were in compliance as follows: 
1.  A udit Committee was in compliance with the provisions of the 
Companies Act and SEBI (LODR) Regulations, 2015 with effect from 16
th May 2025.
2.  Nomination and Remuneration Committee was in compliance 
with the provisions of the Companies Act and SEBI (LODR) Regulations, 2015 with effect from 24
th May 2025.
3.  Stak eholders Relations Committee and Risk Management 
Committee was in compliance with the SEBI (LODR) Regulations, 2015 with effect from 17
th April 2025.
(c)  In absence of r equisite number of Independent Directors, the 
Company was not in compliance with the Section 135 of the Companies Act, 2013 pertaining to composition of Corporate 
Social Responsibility upto 16.04.2025.Corporate Social Responsibility Committee was in compliance with 
the provisions of the Companies Act, 2013, with effect from 17
th April 
2025.
